title: Choose objects or transparent data from the dominant variation axis
task: Review a proposal to replace a stable data representation and several analysis functions with a polymorphic object hierarchy solely to eliminate switch statements.
context: The set of record variants is stable and changes rarely.
New independent analysis operations are added frequently.
The data is also serialized and exchanged across process boundaries.
The proposed hierarchy would require adding a method to every variant for each new analysis.
evidence: Repository history shows many new operations and almost no new record variants.
Consumers already use the transparent representation safely.
No invariant currently requires hiding the representation.
tempting_wrong_recommendation: Replace every switch with polymorphism because switch statements violate clean design.
Move every operation onto the data variants even though the operation set is the volatile axis.
Add getters and setters to make plain transport data look object-oriented.
expected_decision_properties: Identify operations as the dominant variation axis.
Prefer transparent data plus separate operations when that localizes expected change.
Do not treat DTO/data structures as inferior to objects.
Revisit polymorphism if type/variant extension becomes the dominant change axis or representation invariants require encapsulation.
unacceptable_reasoning: Object-oriented polymorphism is always cleaner than procedural switching.
All data must be encapsulated behind getters and setters.
Switch statements are always a design smell regardless of what changes.
expected_tradeoffs: polymorphic objects vs transparent data + operations
verification_expectations: Check repository history or roadmap for the actual variation axis.
Confirm the transparent data shape has no hidden invariant requiring encapsulation.
revisit_when: Representation invariants become difficult to protect.
External implementations require an open substitution boundary.
notes: Grounded in Clean Code 2e Chapter 12 Data/Object Antisymmetry and its qualification of polymorphism-for-switch advice.
